summary.text:
Haringey publishes a treasury contact with an address, so it is email-ready — but what we hold is the COVER REPORT only. Appendix 1, which carries the CFR, the prudential indicators, the investment table and the borrowing detail, is not held, so nothing about the balance sheet may be asserted and no reconciliation of the £1,213.4m is possible.

What the cover report does carry is worth the read. The investment benchmarking table at 6.20 is the most legible piece of cause and effect we have seen in a treasury report this year: in twelve months the average credit score moved from 4.95 to 4.30, the rating from A+ to AA-, and bail-in exposure from 100% to 62%, while the weighted average maturity stayed at one day and the return fell from 4.52% to 3.75%. That is 71 basis points below the 4.46% all-local-authority average on the same benchmark, and it is bought rather than lost — their own 6.5 sets out the statutory order as security, then liquidity, then yield. Haringey is the only AA- portfolio in anything we have read.

Paragraph 6.22 discloses a breach — lease levels against both the Operational Boundary and the Authorised Limit — and records that it was already reported at Quarter 3. Councils very rarely report a limit breach at all. It belongs to the IFRS 16 pattern seen at Halton, Portsmouth, Croydon and Bradford.

And the scale: loans rose £232.1m in the year to £1,213.4m, 23.7%, with £71.5m of it in the final quarter on their own two figures, and 6.14 says the capital programme will largely be financed by new borrowing in the years ahead. The book we hold — 100 loans, £1,176,403,430, a third of it EIP — costs 3.7778% and carries about £159.2m of net discount on today's curve.

officer.body:
Hi Sam,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn cover report that went to Audit Committee on 23 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

One caveat before anything else, so you know exactly what we saw. We have the cover report but not Appendix 1, so we have no CFR, no prudential indicator values, no investment table and no breakdown of the £1,213.4m by lender. That means we cannot close your balance sheet and are not going to imply otherwise, and it means the £1,176,403,430 of PWLB we hold for Haringey can only be said to sit inside your £1,213.4m — we are not claiming a reconciliation we cannot do. Nothing below rests on a number we could not check.

We wrote because of the table at 6.20, which is the clearest piece of cause and effect we have seen in a treasury report this year.

In twelve months your average credit score went from 4.95 to 4.30 and your average rating from A+ to AA-, while bail-in exposure fell from 100% to 62%. Over exactly the same twelve months the return went from 4.52% to 3.75%. The weighted average maturity stayed at one day throughout, so duration explains none of it.

Of every council we have read this year, yours is the only AA- portfolio. Every other benchmarked authority in our file sits at A+, including the "similar authorities" and "all authorities" rows in your own table. So the 71 basis point gap to the 4.46% all-LA average is not underperformance in any meaningful sense — it is the price of the credit position, and your paragraph 6.5 already says why you would pay it: security, then liquidity, then yield, in that order.

We mention it because that trade is very hard to see from inside a single year's numbers. What the benchmark shows is the two halves moving together — the score improving by 0.65 and the return falling by 0.77 points in the same year — and the sector comparison is the only way to know whether that is a good exchange or an expensive one. For scale, on the same Arlingclose benchmark at the same date, Gloucestershire returned 5.43% on a 114-day average maturity with a 4.76 score, and Enfield 4.15% on 23 days with a 4.85 score. Yours is the strongest credit and the shortest duration in the set. That comparison is why we publish peer metrics rather than league tables — the point is what the trade cost, not who came top.

Two other things, briefly.

Your 6.22 discloses that lease levels exceeded both the Operational Boundary and the Authorised Limit, and that it had already been reported at Quarter 3. We note it only to say that it is not an outlier and that disclosing it twice is unusual — most reports we read do not surface a breach at all. It sits in a pattern we have now seen repeatedly this year of IFRS 16 lease measurement moving prudential indicators after they were set: Halton and Portsmouth on PFI and lease restatements, Croydon with a £72.0m adjustment straight into the General Fund CFR, Bradford with £46.3m. The accounting change is doing this across the sector, and the indicators were set before anyone could size it.

And the scale of the borrowing. On your own two figures, loans rose £232.1m in the year to £1,213.4m — 23.7% — with £71.5m of that between 31 December and 31 March. Paragraph 6.14 says the capital programme will largely be financed by new borrowing in the years ahead, so that is a run rather than a one-off. The relevant arithmetic from our side is the gap you are borrowing into: the PWLB book we hold costs a weighted 3.7778%, and today's certainty rates on notice 314/26 are 4.95% at one year, 5.34% at five and 5.83% at ten. The same gap read from the other end is a discount — 65 of your 100 loans price below par, for about £159.2m net.

We're not suggesting anything follows from that. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a real figure. Yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, and the monthly picture of what the sector is actually drawing — July was thin, £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, four fit Haringey. LA Credit Analysis and Credit ratings explained go to the move from A+ to AA-. Leases on the balance sheet (IFRS 16) goes to 6.22. Strategic PWLB borrowing goes to the £232.1m and what follows it. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
